transitivity: both — transitive (they *attacked* the village), intransitive (the enemy *attacked* at dawn)
gloss: To use violence against a person, place, or army in order to hurt them or take control.
examples: Two men *attacked* him outside the bar.
A wounded animal will *attack* anyone who comes close.
The base was *attacked* twice in the same week.

gloss: To attack someone violently, especially in a way that is a crime.
examples: He was arrested for *assaulting* a police officer.
Two teenagers *assaulted* the driver and took his keys.
Nobody who *assaults* a stranger on the street walks away free.
contrast: The silent *au* sounds like *aw*: uh-SAWLT, never "uh-SALT".

gloss: To attack someone suddenly from a hidden position.
examples: Rebels *ambushed* the convoy on a mountain road.
They planned to *ambush* the patrol at the bridge.
The soldiers had been *ambushed* before they reached the border.
contrast: Ends in *-sh*, so the third person adds *-es*: *ambushes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*invade* a country), intransitive (the army *invaded* in spring)
gloss: To enter a country or area with an army in order to take control of it.
examples: The Romans *invaded* Britain almost two thousand years ago.
No small country expects a neighbor to *invade* it overnight.
The island has been *invaded* three times in its history.
contrast: No preposition after it: *invaded Poland*, not "invaded into Poland".

gloss: To make a sudden attack on a place, or to enter it suddenly as police looking for something.
examples: Police *raided* the warehouse just before dawn.
Agents *raid* the club almost every summer.
The apartment had already been *raided* twice that year.

gloss: To attack a place continuously with bombs or heavy gunfire.
examples: The artillery *bombarded* the city for six days.
Ships out at sea began to *bombard* the coast.
Reporters kept *bombarding* the general with questions.
contrast: Unlike *bomb* /bɑːm/, the second *b* here is pronounced: bahm-BAHRD.

gloss: To attack a building or position suddenly and in force.
examples: Commandos *stormed* the embassy at three in the morning.
Crowds threatened to *storm* the gates of the palace.
The prison was *stormed* by troops after the riot spread.

gloss: To surround a town or fort with an army so that nobody can get in or out.
examples: The army *besieged* the city for nine months.
No modern general wants to *besiege* a place that size.
The fortress had been *besieged* twice before it fell.
contrast: Spelled *-ie-*: *besiege*, *besieged* — not "beseige".

gloss: To take control of a country or people by force.
examples: Spain *conquered* most of South America in a century.
An empire that cannot feed itself cannot *conquer* anyone.
Half of Europe had been *conquered* by the end of that year.
contrast: The *qu* here is just /k/: KAHNG-kur, not "KON-kwer".

gloss: To beat an enemy or opponent in a battle, election, or game.
examples: The rebels *defeated* a much larger army.
A smaller force can *defeat* a big one on the right ground.
Their team has never been *defeated* at home.

gloss: To beat someone by being physically stronger than they are.
examples: Three guards *overpowered* the man at the door.
He is strong enough to *overpower* anyone in the room.
The pilot was *overpowered* by two passengers.

gloss: To be greater in number than another group.
examples: The defenders were *outnumbered* five to one.
Police *outnumbered* the protesters on the square.
Any army that *outnumbers* you still has to feed itself.

gloss: To move into position on every side of a person or place so that they cannot escape.
examples: Troops *surrounded* the building before dawn.
They planned to *surround* the camp and wait.
The house was *surrounded* by the time he woke up.

gloss: To hit someone hard with your closed fist.
examples: He *punched* the other driver in the face.
Don't *punch* a wall when you are angry.
The boxer kept *punching* until the bell rang.
contrast: Ends in *-ch*, so the third person adds *-es*: *punches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*kick* the door), intransitive (the horse *kicks*)
gloss: To hit someone or something with your foot.
examples: Somebody *kicked* the door until the lock broke.
The horse will *kick* if you stand behind it.
He was *kicking* the fence out of sheer frustration.

gloss: To hit someone with the flat, open palm of your hand.
examples: She *slapped* him and walked out.
Never *slap* a child across the face.
He was *slapped* twice before he understood she meant it.
contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *slapped*, *slapping*.

gloss: To hit someone or something sharply with an open hand.
examples: He *smacked* the table so hard the glasses jumped.
Her mother never had to *smack* her twice.
The kid got *smacked* on the wrist for grabbing.

gloss: To push someone or something roughly and suddenly.
examples: Someone *shoved* me from behind in the crowd.
Don't *shove* — there is room for everybody.
They were pushing and *shoving* in front of the gate.
contrast: The *o* sounds like /ʌ/: SHUV, rhyming with *love*, not with *stove*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*wrestle* him to the ground), intransitive (he *wrestled* in college)
gloss: To fight someone by holding them and trying to force them to the ground.
examples: Two officers *wrestled* the gun away from him.
My brother used to *wrestle* in high school.
They were still *wrestling* on the floor when help arrived.
contrast: Both the *w* and the *t* are silent: RES-ul.

gloss: To fight or argue openly with an opposing group.
examples: Protesters *clashed* with police outside city hall.
The two senators *clash* every time they meet.
Fans had been *clashing* in the streets since noon.
contrast: Takes *with*: *clash with the police*; and the third person adds *-es*: *clashes*.

gloss: To fight noisily and without rules, usually in a public place.
examples: Fans *brawled* in the parking lot after the game.
Men who *brawl* in bars usually end up in a cell.
They were *brawling* outside when the police pulled up.

transitivity: both — transitive (*trample* the flowers), intransitive (*trample* on his rights)
gloss: To step heavily on someone or something and crush it.
examples: The crowd *trampled* the fence in the rush to get out.
Cattle will *trample* a garden in minutes.
Two people were *trampled* at the entrance.

gloss: To hit someone or something hard again and again.
examples: Waves *battered* the seawall all night.
The wind kept *battering* the old barn.
She had been *battered* by her husband for years.

gloss: To fight against something harmful in order to stop it or reduce it.
examples: The city *combated* street crime with more patrols.
New laws are meant to *combat* online fraud.
They have been *combating* the same problem for a decade.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *t*: *combated*, *combating* (British often doubles it).

gloss: To make a person, animal, or plant die.
examples: The crash *killed* two passengers.
One hard frost can *kill* every plant in the yard.
Thousands have been *killed* since the war began.

gloss: To kill a person deliberately and unlawfully.
examples: He *murdered* his business partner for the insurance.
Nobody believed she could *murder* anyone.
The witness had been *murdered* a week before the trial.

gloss: To murder an important person, usually for political reasons.
examples: A gunman *assassinated* the ambassador in 1974.
Two groups had plotted to *assassinate* the judge.
The president was *assassinated* in broad daylight.
contrast: Two double letters: *a-ss-a-ss-inate*.

gloss: To kill people or animals in large numbers.
examples: The invaders *slaughtered* everyone in the village.
They *slaughter* the pigs in late autumn.
Whole herds were being *slaughtered* to stop the disease.
contrast: The *gh* is silent, and it does not rhyme with *laughter*: SLAW-tur, LAF-tur.

gloss: To kill a large number of people who cannot defend themselves.
examples: Soldiers *massacred* the prisoners in the courtyard.
No army admits it came to *massacre* civilians.
The villagers had been *massacred* days earlier.
contrast: The *-cre* ending sounds like *-ker*, and the *e* drops before *-ing*: *massacring*.

gloss: To kill someone as a legal punishment.
examples: The state *executed* him thirty years after the crime.
No court in that country can *execute* a minor.
Six prisoners were *executed* that spring.

gloss: To cause someone severe pain deliberately, often to force information out of them.
examples: Guards *tortured* him for three days.
No law allows the army to *torture* prisoners.
He claims he was *tortured* in that camp.

transitivity: both — transitive (*fire* a rifle), intransitive (*fire* at the target)
gloss: To shoot a gun or launch a weapon.
examples: The soldier *fired* twice into the air.
Don't *fire* until you can see the target.
They were *firing* from the roof of the building.
contrast: You *fire at* or *fire on* something; the *e* drops before *-ing*: *firing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*detonate* a bomb), intransitive (the charge *detonated*)
gloss: To make a bomb explode, or to explode.
examples: Engineers *detonated* the old shell in an empty field.
One wire is enough to *detonate* the charge.
The device was *detonated* by remote control.

gloss: To choose a particular person or place to attack or aim at.
examples: The missiles *targeted* the power station.
Thieves often *target* houses with no lights on.
Reporters had been *targeted* by both sides.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* does not double: *targeted*, *targeting*.

gloss: To supply a person or group with weapons.
examples: Foreign governments *armed* both sides of the war.
Nobody wants to *arm* a militia that cannot be controlled.
The men were *armed* with rifles and knives.

transitivity: both — transitive (*disarm* the gunman), intransitive (both sides agreed to *disarm*)
gloss: To take weapons away from a person or group, or to give up weapons.
examples: An officer *disarmed* him without firing a shot.
The treaty required both armies to *disarm*.
The rebels have been *disarmed* under the agreement.

transitivity: both — transitive (*defend* the city), intransitive (they fought to *defend*)
gloss: To protect someone or something from attack.
examples: A hundred men *defended* the bridge for two days.
She learned to *defend* herself as a teenager.
The town had been *defended* by volunteers.
contrast: You *defend* something *against* or *from* an attacker.

transitivity: both — transitive (*guard* the entrance), intransitive (*guard* against mistakes)
gloss: To watch over a place or person in order to keep them safe or stop them escaping.
examples: Two soldiers *guarded* the gate all night.
A dog will *guard* the yard better than a lock.
The building is being *guarded* around the clock.
contrast: Silent *u* after the *g*: *guard*, not "gard".

gloss: To stand between someone and danger so that they are not hurt.
examples: He *shielded* the child with his own body.
Thick walls *shield* the room from the blast.
The witness was *shielded* from the cameras.
contrast: Takes *from*: *shield him from the blast*.

gloss: To build walls or defenses to make a place stronger against attack.
examples: The army *fortified* the hills above the road.
They had three weeks to *fortify* the camp.
Every village along the border has been *fortified*.
contrast: Consonant plus *-y*, so *y* becomes *-ie-*: *fortifies*, *fortified*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*patrol* the border), intransitive (guards *patrol* at night)
gloss: To move regularly around an area to guard it or watch for trouble.
examples: Two jeeps *patrolled* the perimeter every hour.
Soldiers *patrol* the border on foot.
Helicopters were *patrolling* the coast all week.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the *l* doubles: *patrolled*, *patrolling*.

gloss: To make someone decide not to do something, usually by threat or fear.
examples: The fence *deterred* nobody at all.
Heavy fines *deter* most drivers.
He was not *deterred* by the risk of arrest.
contrast: Stress on the last syllable, so the *r* doubles: *deterred*, *deterring*; *deter someone from doing something*.

gloss: To drive an attacking force back and away.
examples: The garrison *repelled* three assaults in one night.
A small force can *repel* a bigger one from high ground.
The attack was *repelled* before it reached the wall.
contrast: Stress on the last syllable, so the *l* doubles: *repelled*, *repelling*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*resist* arrest), intransitive (the town did not *resist*)
gloss: To fight against something or refuse to accept it.
examples: The villagers *resisted* for nearly a month.
He was charged with *resisting* arrest.
Some of the old families have *resisted* every change.
contrast: No preposition: *resist the pressure*, not "resist to the pressure".

gloss: To stop someone or something from passing or from succeeding.
examples: Protesters *blocked* the main highway for hours.
One senator can *block* the whole bill.
The road has been *blocked* since the fighting started.

transitivity: both — transitive (*deflect* a blow), intransitive (the bullet *deflected*)
gloss: To turn a blow, a shot, or an attack away from its target.
examples: His arm *deflected* most of the blow.
The minister tried to *deflect* every hard question.
The shot had been *deflected* by the door frame.

transitivity: both — transitive (*dodge* the punch), intransitive (he *dodged* to the left)
gloss: To move quickly aside to avoid being hit.
examples: He *dodged* the first punch and threw one back.
You cannot *dodge* a bullet, whatever the movies say.
She spent the whole interview *dodging* the question.
contrast: The silent *e* drops before *-ing*: *dodging*, not "dodgeing".

transitivity: both — transitive (*shelter* refugees), intransitive (*shelter* from the shelling)
gloss: To give someone a safe place to stay, or to take cover yourself.
examples: A church *sheltered* forty families that winter.
They had nowhere to *shelter* when the shelling began.
Hundreds were *sheltering* in the subway stations.

transitivity: both — transitive (*counter* the argument), intransitive ("Not true," he *countered*)
gloss: To reply to an attack or argument with one of your own.
examples: The general *countered* with an attack on the flank.
Nothing he says can *counter* that evidence.
They were *countering* every claim within an hour.

gloss: To do something harmful to someone because they harmed you first.
examples: The other side *retaliated* within hours.
If we hit them now, they will *retaliate*.
He was fired for *retaliating* against a witness.
contrast: Takes *against* or *for*: *retaliate against a rival*, *retaliate for the raid*.

gloss: To punish someone for a wrong done to you or to a person you care about.
examples: He swore he would *avenge* his brother's death.
The family *avenged* the insult a year later.
She died believing her son had been *avenged*.
contrast: *Avenge* is the verb; *revenge* is normally the noun: *take revenge*, but *avenge a death*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*threaten* a witness), intransitive (the clouds *threatened*)
gloss: To say that you will hurt or punish someone if they do not do what you want.
examples: He *threatened* the clerk with a knife.
They *threaten* to close the plant every spring.
Two jurors said they had been *threatened*.
contrast: *Threaten to do* something, or *threaten someone with* something.

gloss: To frighten or hurt someone weaker, again and again.
examples: Older boys *bullied* him for two years.
Nobody should have to *bully* a coworker to get respect.
She was being *bullied* online every night.
contrast: Consonant plus *-y*, so *y* becomes *-ie-*: *bullies*, *bullied* — but *bullying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To annoy or attack someone repeatedly over a period of time.
examples: Guards *harassed* the drivers at every checkpoint.
He was accused of *harassing* two employees.
She has been *harassed* by phone calls for months.
contrast: One *r*, two *s*'s, and the third person adds *-es*: *harasses*.

gloss: To frighten a person or group badly by using violence or threats.
examples: One gang *terrorized* the whole neighborhood.
They used the dogs to *terrorize* the prisoners.
The village had been *terrorized* for a year.
contrast: American spelling uses *-ize*: *terrorize* (British *terrorise*).

gloss: To force someone to do something by threatening to reveal a secret about them.
examples: Someone *blackmailed* him over the old photographs.
They tried to *blackmail* the mayor into signing.
He admitted *blackmailing* two former clients.

gloss: To get money or something else from someone by using threats or force.
examples: The gang *extorted* money from every shop on the block.
They tried to *extort* a confession out of him.
Thousands had been *extorted* before anyone complained.
contrast: Takes *from*: *extort money from a shop owner*.

gloss: To make someone do something by using force or threats.
examples: Officers *coerced* him into signing the statement.
You cannot *coerce* a witness and expect the case to stand.
The confession had clearly been *coerced*.
contrast: *Coerce someone into doing* something; the *oe* is two syllables: koh-URS.

gloss: To make someone do something they do not want to do.
examples: Hunger *forced* the defenders to surrender.
Nobody can *force* you to testify against your husband.
Hundreds of families are being *forced* out of the valley.
contrast: *Force someone to do* something — with *to*, unlike *make someone do*.

gloss: To try hard to persuade someone to do something they are unwilling to do.
examples: His family *pressured* him into dropping the case.
Don't let them *pressure* you into an answer today.
Witnesses say they were *pressured* by both lawyers.
contrast: *Pressure someone into* doing something, or *to do* it.

gloss: To treat a person cruelly or violently, or to use power unfairly.
examples: He *abused* his position to silence critics.
No one should *abuse* an animal like that.
She had been *abused* as a child.
contrast: The verb ends in /z/ (uh-BYOOZ); the noun *abuse* ends in /s/ (uh-BYOOS).

gloss: To argue about small, unimportant things.
examples: The two of them *bickered* all the way home.
Neighbors *bicker* over a foot of fence.
They have been *bickering* about money since January.
contrast: Takes *over* or *about*: *bicker over the bill*.

gloss: To formally argue that something is wrong, or to compete for something.
examples: The family *contested* the will in court.
He plans to *contest* the result of the election.
Every inch of that border has been *contested* for years.
contrast: The verb is kun-TEST; the noun *contest* is KAHN-test, stressed on the first syllable.

gloss: To say cruel things to someone in order to make them angry or upset.
examples: The other players *taunted* him about the missed shot.
Don't *taunt* a man who has nothing left to lose.
He was *taunting* the crowd from the far side of the fence.

gloss: To make fun of someone in a cruel way so that others laugh at them.
examples: Newspapers *ridiculed* the plan for weeks.
It is easy to *ridicule* an idea you never had to test.
His accent was *ridiculed* by half the class.

gloss: To criticize someone or something publicly and strongly.
examples: The mayor *denounced* the attack the same evening.
Church leaders continue to *denounce* the new law.
He was *denounced* by his own party.

gloss: To say very strongly that something or someone is wrong or evil.
examples: Both governments *condemned* the bombing.
It costs nothing to *condemn* violence in a speech.
He was *condemned* to death by a military court.
contrast: The final *n* is silent: kun-DEM — though you hear it in *condemnation*.

gloss: To treat a group of people cruelly and unfairly, giving them no freedom.
examples: That regime *oppressed* its own people for forty years.
No government admits that it *oppresses* anyone.
The minority had been *oppressed* for generations.
contrast: Two *p*'s, two *s*'s, and the third person adds *-es*: *oppresses*.

ru: противостоять; открыто выступать против; смело встречать
gloss: To face someone or something difficult directly instead of avoiding it.
examples: She finally *confronted* her boss about the missing hours.
Sooner or later you have to *confront* the problem.
He was *confronted* by two men in the parking lot.

gloss: To question whether something is right, or to invite someone to fight or compete.
examples: He *challenged* the ruling in a higher court.
Nobody dared to *challenge* the old man's authority.
The result is being *challenged* by three candidates.
contrast: *Challenge someone to* something: *challenged him to a fight*.

gloss: To refuse openly to obey a person, rule, or order.
examples: Thousands *defied* the curfew that night.
Few officers will *defy* a direct order.
She has *defied* her family since she was sixteen.
contrast: Consonant plus *-y*, so *y* becomes *-ie-*: *defies*, *defied* — but *defying* keeps the *y*.

ru: участвовать в демонстрации, выходить на демонстрацию
gloss: To march or gather in public with other people to show that you support or oppose something.
examples: Students *demonstrated* outside the courthouse for a week.
Thousands plan to *demonstrate* against the new law.
They were *demonstrating* peacefully when the police arrived.
contrast: In this sense it takes *against* or *for*: *demonstrate against the war*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*rally* supporters), intransitive (the crowd *rallied* downtown)
gloss: To come together, or bring people together, to support a cause or a leader.
examples: Farmers *rallied* on the steps of the capitol.
He can still *rally* a crowd in any small town.
The party has *rallied* behind its new leader.
contrast: Consonant plus *-y*: *rallies*, *rallied*, but *rallying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*picket* the factory), intransitive (workers *picketed* all week)
gloss: To stand outside a workplace in protest, usually to stop people going in.
examples: Nurses *picketed* the hospital for eleven days.
They plan to *picket* every store in the chain.
Drivers have been *picketing* the depot since Monday.
contrast: Stress on the first syllable, so the *t* stays single: *picketed*, *picketing*.

gloss: To refuse to buy from, deal with, or take part in something as a protest.
examples: Shoppers *boycotted* the company for a year.
Two parties plan to *boycott* the election.
The games were *boycotted* by a dozen countries.

gloss: To join a violent crowd that fights, breaks things, or attacks the police.
examples: Prisoners *rioted* after the visits were canceled.
Crowds *riot* when the price of bread doubles.
People had been *rioting* in the capital for three nights.
contrast: Two syllables, RY-ut, and the *t* stays single: *rioted*, *rioting*.

gloss: To fight against a government or authority, or to refuse to accept its control.
examples: The colonies *rebelled* against the crown.
Teenagers *rebel* against whatever their parents believe.
Half the army had *rebelled* by the end of the month.
contrast: The verb is ri-BEL; the noun *rebel* is REB-ul. Stress on the last syllable doubles the *l*: *rebelled*.

gloss: To rise up violently against a ruler or government.
examples: The peasants *revolted* after the third bad harvest.
Whole provinces may *revolt* if the tax goes through.
Sailors were *revolting* in two ports at once.
contrast: Takes *against*: *revolt against the king*.

gloss: To work in an organized way over time to change something or win support.
examples: She *campaigned* for prison reform for twenty years.
They *campaign* against the pipeline every summer.
He has been *campaigning* since the spring.
contrast: Silent *g*: kam-PAYN. Takes *for* or *against*.

gloss: To surround a port, road, or country so that nothing can go in or out.
examples: Warships *blockaded* the harbor for six months.
Farmers threatened to *blockade* the highway with tractors.
The city has been *blockaded* since the spring.
contrast: Stress on the second syllable: blah-KAYD, unlike the verb *block*.

gloss: To take control of a place by force and stay there.
examples: Troops *occupied* the airport within an hour.
Students plan to *occupy* the administration building.
The country was *occupied* for four years.
contrast: Consonant plus *-y*: *occupies*, *occupied*, but *occupying*.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the garrison *surrendered*), transitive (*surrender* your weapons)
gloss: To stop fighting and accept that the enemy has won.
examples: The last unit *surrendered* in early May.
They would rather burn the bridge than *surrender* it.
He turned himself in, *surrendering* his passport at the door.
contrast: Takes *to*: *surrendered to the police*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*concede* the point), intransitive (he *conceded* that night)
gloss: To admit that you have lost, or to allow an opponent something.
examples: The governor *conceded* an hour after the polls closed.
He will never *concede* that he was wrong.
Two districts had already been *conceded*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*obey* an order), intransitive (the dog *obeys*)
gloss: To do what a person, law, or order tells you to do.
examples: The soldiers *obeyed* without a word.
You have to *obey* the same rules as everyone else.
He claimed he was only *obeying* orders.
contrast: The *y* follows a vowel, so it never changes: *obeys*, *obeyed*. No preposition: *obey the law*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*disobey* an order), intransitive (he *disobeyed* again)
gloss: To refuse to do what you are told to do by a person or law.
examples: Two officers *disobeyed* the order to fire.
Nobody in that unit would dare *disobey* him.
He was punished for *disobeying* a direct command.

transitivity: both — transitive (*evacuate* the town), intransitive (residents *evacuated* at noon)
gloss: To move people out of a dangerous place, or to leave it.
examples: The army *evacuated* four villages near the front.
Families were told to *evacuate* before dark.
The building had been *evacuated* an hour earlier.

gloss: To leave a place, thing, or person that you are responsible for, and not return.
examples: The crew *abandoned* the ship at midnight.
They refused to *abandon* the wounded.
The position had been *abandoned* days before.
contrast: The final *n* does not double: *abandoned*, not "abandonned".

transitivity: both — transitive (*desert* your post), intransitive (two men *deserted*)
gloss: To leave the army without permission, or to leave someone who needs you.
examples: Half the regiment *deserted* that winter.
A man who would *desert* his friends will desert you too.
He was shot for *deserting* his post.
contrast: The verb is di-ZURT; the noun *desert* (the Sahara) is DEZ-urt.

transitivity: both — intransitive (he *enlisted* at eighteen), transitive (*enlist* their support)
gloss: To join the armed forces, or to get someone's help.
examples: My grandfather *enlisted* in 1942.
Thousands *enlist* every year straight out of school.
She has *enlisted* two neighbors to help with the petition.

gloss: To move soldiers or equipment into position for action.
examples: The general *deployed* two brigades along the river.
They may *deploy* more troops by the weekend.
He has been *deployed* overseas three times.
contrast: The *y* follows a vowel, so it stays: *deployed*, *deploying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*command* a regiment), intransitive (he was born to *command*)
gloss: To be in charge of soldiers, or to order someone to do something.
examples: She *commanded* a unit of two hundred men.
He can *command* a room without raising his voice.
The ship was *commanded* by an officer of twenty-six.
contrast: The *a* is /æ/ as in *hand*: kuh-MAND, not "kuh-MAHND".

transitivity: both — transitive (*mobilize* the reserves), intransitive (the army *mobilized*)
gloss: To gather soldiers or supporters and make them ready for action.
examples: The country *mobilized* within forty-eight hours.
Both sides are trying to *mobilize* young voters.
Reserves had already been *mobilized* by then.
contrast: American spelling uses *-ize*: *mobilize* (British *mobilise*).

gloss: To harm someone who trusts you, especially by helping their enemies.
examples: A neighbor *betrayed* the family to the soldiers.
He would never *betray* the people who hid him.
She felt *betrayed* by everyone in the office.
contrast: The *y* follows a vowel, so it stays: *betrayed*, *betraying*.

gloss: To plan something harmful or illegal secretly with other people.
examples: Four officers *conspired* to overthrow the government.
Nobody could prove the two men *conspire* at all.
They were charged with *conspiring* against the state.
contrast: Takes *against* or *with*, and *to do* something: *conspired to kill him*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*plot* a coup), intransitive (they *plotted* for months)
gloss: To make a secret plan to do something harmful.
examples: Two generals *plotted* to seize the capital.
Prisoners *plot* escapes they will never attempt.
He had been *plotting* against his own brother.
contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the *t* doubles: *plotted*, *plotting*.

gloss: To set a place or people free from an enemy or from control.
examples: Allied troops *liberated* the city in August.
No army can *liberate* a country against its will.
The camp was *liberated* a week before the war ended.

transitivity: both — transitive (*ally* yourself with them), intransitive (the tribes *allied*)
gloss: To join with another person or country for a shared purpose, usually against someone.
examples: Two small states *allied* against their neighbor.
He chose to *ally* himself with the reformers.
The country had long been *allied* with Britain.
contrast: The verb is uh-LY; the noun *ally* is AL-eye. *Y* becomes *-ie-*: *allies*, *allied*.

transitivity: both — transitive (a threat *unites* people), intransitive (the parties *united*)
gloss: To join people or groups together so that they act as one.
examples: The invasion *united* parties that had hated each other.
Nothing will *unite* that town again.
The factions are *uniting* behind a single candidate.
contrast: Begins with a /j/ sound: yoo-NYT, so it takes *a*, not *an*.

gloss: To bring a person or group under control by force.
examples: Three officers *subdued* the man on the platform.
It took a year to *subdue* the last of the rebels.
He was *subdued* and handcuffed within seconds.
contrast: The silent *e* drops before *-ing*: *subduing*.

gloss: To hold someone back physically, or to stop yourself from acting.
examples: Two friends *restrained* him before he swung again.
Try to *restrain* yourself when he starts shouting.
The suspect was *restrained* on the ground.

gloss: To stop a protest, a report, or a feeling by force or authority.
examples: Troops *suppressed* the uprising in a single day.
Governments that *suppress* the press rarely stop there.
The report had been *suppressed* for two years.
contrast: Two *p*'s and two *s*'s; the third person adds *-es*: *suppresses*.

gloss: To treat people cruelly over a long time because of their race, religion, or beliefs.
examples: The empire *persecuted* Christians for three centuries.
Any state can *persecute* a minority and call it order.
They were *persecuted* until they finally left the country.
contrast: *Persecute* (преследовать, притеснять) is not *prosecute* (привлекать к суду).

gloss: To take someone to a police station because they are suspected of a crime.
examples: Police *arrested* four people at the protest.
They can *arrest* you for that in this state.
He has been *arrested* twice this year.
contrast: Takes *for*: *arrested for theft*.

gloss: To keep someone in official custody and not let them leave.
examples: Border guards *detained* him for six hours.
They can *detain* a suspect for two days without charges.
Dozens are still being *detained* without trial.

ru: заключать в тюрьму, сажать в тюрьму
gloss: To put someone in prison and keep them there.
examples: The regime *imprisoned* hundreds of journalists.
You cannot *imprison* a man for what he thinks.
He was *imprisoned* for eleven years.
contrast: The final *n* does not double: *imprisoned*, *imprisoning*.

ru: сажать в тюрьму, заключать под стражу
gloss: To put someone in jail as a punishment.
examples: The court *jailed* him for five years.
They rarely *jail* first offenders here.
She was *jailed* for refusing to name her source.

gloss: To question someone closely and for a long time, often in an aggressive way.
examples: Agents *interrogated* him through the night.
They plan to *interrogate* every man on the list.
He was being *interrogated* when his lawyer arrived.
contrast: Double *r*: *interrogate*.

ru: привлекать к суду, преследовать в судебном порядке
transitivity: both — transitive (*prosecute* a case), intransitive (the state declined to *prosecute*)
gloss: To officially charge someone with a crime and take them to court.
examples: The city *prosecuted* him for assault.
They decided not to *prosecute* the driver.
Trespassers will be *prosecuted*.

gloss: To decide officially in court that someone is guilty of a crime.
examples: The jury *convicted* him in under an hour.
It is hard to *convict* anyone on that evidence.
She has never been *convicted* of anything.
contrast: The verb is kun-VIKT; the noun *convict* (a prisoner) is KAHN-vikt. Takes *of*: *convicted of fraud*.

ru: подавать в суд на, судиться с
transitivity: both — transitive (*sue* the company), intransitive (they threatened to *sue*)
gloss: To take legal action against a person or company in a court.
examples: He *sued* his employer for wrongful dismissal.
If they print that, she will *sue*.
The city is being *sued* by three families.
contrast: Keep the *u* but drop the *e* before *-ing*: *suing*, not "sueing".

gloss: To make sure that a law or rule is obeyed.
examples: Nobody *enforced* the curfew in the old town.
It is one thing to pass a law and another to *enforce* it.
The ban is being *enforced* for the first time.

gloss: To break a law, rule, or agreement.
examples: Both sides *violated* the ceasefire within a week.
That order would *violate* international law.
He was arrested for *violating* the restraining order.

transitivity: both — transitive (*mediate* a dispute), intransitive (she agreed to *mediate*)
gloss: To help two sides in a conflict reach an agreement.
examples: A retired judge *mediated* the dispute.
Neighbors asked the church to *mediate* between them.
The talks were *mediated* by two foreign ministers.
contrast: Takes *between*: *mediate between the two sides*.

gloss: To become involved in a conflict in order to change what is happening.
examples: A passerby *intervened* before it turned into a fight.
Nobody expects the army to *intervene* now.
Two governments have been *intervening* on opposite sides.
contrast: Takes *in* or *between*: *intervene in the conflict*.

transitivity: both — intransitive (the fight *escalated*), transitive (*escalate* the conflict)
gloss: To become more serious or violent, or to make something do so.
examples: The argument *escalated* into a brawl.
One more raid could *escalate* the whole thing.
Tensions have been *escalating* since the election.
contrast: Takes *into*: *escalated into a war*.

gloss: To make a bomb safe, or to make a dangerous situation calmer.
examples: A team *defused* the device in the parking garage.
One calm officer can *defuse* a crowd like that.
The crisis was *defused* by a phone call.
contrast: *Defuse* (обезвредить) is not *diffuse* (рассеивать).

gloss: To fight hard against someone or something, especially when you are losing.
examples: She *struggled* with the man until he let go.
They still *struggle* for basic rights in that region.
He has been *struggling* against the ruling for years.
contrast: Takes *with*, *against*, or *for*: *struggle against the current*.

gloss: To catch someone in a place or situation they cannot get out of.
examples: The fire *trapped* twelve people on the third floor.
They planned to *trap* the patrol in the canyon.
Two soldiers were *trapped* behind enemy lines for a month.
contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *trapped*, *trapping*.

gloss: To take control of a plane, ship, or truck by force.
examples: Four men *hijacked* the plane over the Atlantic.
Thieves often *hijack* trucks on that stretch of road.
The bus was *hijacked* twenty miles from the border.

gloss: To take a person away by force and hold them, usually for money.
examples: Gunmen *kidnapped* two engineers near the port.
They threatened to *kidnap* his daughter.
He was *kidnapped* on his way home from work.
contrast: The *p* doubles in American English: *kidnapped*, *kidnapping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*loot* a store), intransitive (crowds were *looting*)
gloss: To steal things from shops or homes during a war or riot.
examples: Crowds *looted* every store on the avenue.
Soldiers are not supposed to *loot* the towns they take.
The museum had already been *looted*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*disperse* the crowd), intransitive (the crowd *dispersed*)
gloss: To make a crowd break up and go away, or to break up and go away.
examples: Police *dispersed* the protesters with tear gas.
The crowd refused to *disperse*.
By midnight everyone had *dispersed*.

ru: перебегать (к врагу), дезертировать; бежать из страны
gloss: To leave your country or party and join the opposing one.
examples: A colonel *defected* two days before the offensive.
Dozens of officials *defect* every year.
He has *defected* to the other side and taken the files with him.
contrast: The verb is di-FEKT; the noun *defect* (a flaw) is DEE-fekt. Takes *to*: *defected to the West*.
